name: These
confidence_why: Yip's 2004 phonology of These describes three level and two contour tones that contrast both lexically and in verb aspect, and Stevenson's 1970s-80s Tese work sheets independently note a probable three-tone system, so the tonal classification is uncontested, but both accounts are short and preliminary and no full grammar of the language exists.
catalog_citation: Yip, May. 2004. Phonology of the These language. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 93-117. Entebbe: SIL-Sudan.
catalog_locator: Sec. 3 'Tone', printed p. 108 = p. 114 = p. 15 of the extracted article PDF (whose pages run printed 94-117 then 93 last); saved under the copy we hold/ ( article, 9e37766231e874f16336ccf365dc4c1c volume)
catalog_quote: The These language has three level tones and two contour tones. The level tones are High, Mid and Low. The contour tones are rising and falling. Low tone and High tone are the most common ones, while Mid tone is less common. The falling tone only occurs at the last syllable, and rising tone is rare in my data. More study is needed for tones. ... Tone is distinctive at the lexical level. Example (40) shows the contrast of tones. ... Tone also distinguishes the verb aspect. For instance, High tone with a doubled consonant distinguishes: --the 1st, person singular present verb form from the 1st person singular past verb form
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tese is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus falling and rising contours; tone is lexically contrastive and marks verb aspect (with consonant gemination). The article, the only phonological description of the language, contains no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Falling tone restricted to the final syllable; rising tone rare; mid tone less common and left unmarked in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone and verb-aspect tone; citation-form data from Khartoum-based speakers. Silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Yip's 'These' = Tesei Umm Danab = Glottolog tese1238 (dialect teis1234). Glottolog folds 'Keiga Jirru' (keig1243) into tese1238 as a dialect and lists it as an alternative name, following Ethnologue; Blench 2013 and Stevenson's notes treat Keiga Jirru (autonym Doni) as a distinct third Temein language, and Yip herself says the These people regard These and Keiga Jirru as one language in different dialects. Not to be confused with Keiga (Kadu family, keig1242).

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Yip 2004 statement (tone language; no stress statement); independent and earlier (1970s data). Adds nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stevenson's first-hand notes (informants 1976-79, Khartoum) treat Tese as having a probable three-tone system with tone marked on the wordlist forms; nothing is said about Tese word stress. The only 'stress' remark concerns the Arabic source word of the loan 'mat'. The Bender First-Fifth 100 work sheets (1983-86) and the 'additional items' pages are tone-marked wordlists only.
new_statements.identity_note: Work 1 is explicitly Teisei umm Danab (self-name Tese), hill range NE of Kadugli, Temein-type speakers, informants 1976-79 = Glottolog tese1238. Work 2 describes the Temein group with all examples from Temein proper [teq] and Jirru (Keiga Jirru/Doni) in italics; Teis-um-Danab is not named anywhere in the 1966 book. Work 0 is only Blench's index page; the comparative wordlist it links treats Temein, Tese and Keiga Jirru as three separate columns.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another on These itself: Yip 2004 (three level + two contour tones, lexical and grammatical tone, no mention of stress) and Stevenson's 1970s-80s Tese notes (probable three-tone system, tone-marked wordlists, no stress statement) agree. The only tension is at the group level: Tucker & Bryan 1966, reporting Stevenson's Temein-proper data, say Stevenson 'notes the existence of both tone and stress' without any placement rule, whereas Stevenson's own Tese notes and Yip's These phonology speak only of tone; and Blench 2013 (already held by the project) records Dimmendaal's view that a High/Low plus downstep analysis fits the Temein tone systems better than three levels. None of this yields a stress placement for These.
